title: Sources of Ancient History: Inscriptions and Coins

cards.b: Ancient India has few year-by-year chronicles. Historians rebuild the past from inscriptions, coins, monuments, foreign accounts and literature. Prelims loves matching an inscription to its ruler and language.

Epigraphy studies inscriptions; numismatics studies coins; palaeography studies old scripts. Inscriptions on rock, pillar, copper plate and temple wall record grants, victories and orders. Coins date events, show trade and rulers’ religion.

James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi in 1837, helped by bilingual Greek-Indian coins, and read “Devanampiya Piyadasi” on Ashokan edicts. Only in 1915 did the Maski edict (Karnataka) name Ashoka directly. Brahmi runs left to right; Kharosthi right to left, used in the north-west.

Hathigumpha (Kharavela of Kalinga, Odisha, Jaina king); Junagadh rock inscription (Rudradaman, c. 150 CE, first long Sanskrit inscription, Sudarshana lake); Allahabad Pillar (Samudragupta, by Harisena); Aihole (Pulakeshin II, by Ravikirti, 634 CE); Mehrauli iron pillar (Chandra); Uttaramerur (Parantaka Chola, village assembly rules); Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (Vaishnavism).

Punch-marked coins (karshapana) are the oldest, silver, c. 6th century BCE. Indo-Greek kings first put names and portraits on coins. Kushanas issued gold; Guptas issued fine gold dinaras (Samudragupta playing the veena). Satavahana lead coins show ships. Hoards show trade with Rome.

Megasthenes (Indica, in Chandragupta’s court), Fa-Hien (Gupta India), Hsuan Tsang (Harsha), Al-Biruni (Kitab-ul-Hind, 11th century), Kalhana’s Rajatarangini (12th century), the only real historical text from ancient India. Sangam poems and Kautilya’s Arthashastra complete the picture.

Royal inscriptions praise kings; they may exaggerate victory. Many texts were later edited. Archaeologists cross-check, for example the Greek claim of Chandragupta meeting Seleucus with the Mauryan record. No source gives a full picture alone.

The ASI’s Epigraphy branch is at Mysuru; “Epigraphia Indica” publishes finds. The Indian Treasure Trove Act, 1878 requires reporting coin hoards. The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972 regulates sale of antiquities. Classical language status for Tamil and others depends on old inscriptions and texts.
